title: Numbers 14:11–25
context: The LORD threatens to strike the people with pestilence and make a greater nation from Moses. Moses intercedes, appealing to God’s reputation among the nations and to the character God revealed at Sinai, and asks him to pardon. The LORD pardons, yet swears that none of the men who saw his glory and still tested him will see the land, except Caleb, who followed him fully. Israel must turn back toward the wilderness.

verses.text: The LORD said to Moses, “How long will this people despise me? How long will they not believe in me, for all the signs which I have worked among them?
verses.arminianNotes: God asks how long the people will despise him and refuse to believe despite all his signs. The core sin is unbelief in the face of clear evidence. Arminian readers stress that such unbelief is real resistance to God’s gracious dealings.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also identify unbelief as the root sin, as Hebrews 3:19 says. Signs alone do not produce faith in a hardened heart. This is shared ground.

verses.text: I will strike them with the pestilence, and disinherit them, and will make of you a nation greater and mightier than they.”
verses.arminianNotes: God threatens to destroy Israel and make a greater nation from Moses. Classical Arminian readers, who affirm God’s exhaustive foreknowledge, typically read the threat as a genuine statement of what the people deserve, given in a way that calls forth Moses’ intercession.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise read the threat as declaring what justice deserves. They also see it as a test that draws out Moses’ role as mediator. Both traditions reject the idea that God was caught off guard.

verses.text: Moses said to the LORD, “Then the Egyptians will hear it; for you brought up this people in your might from among them.
verses.arminianNotes: Moses begins by appealing to God’s reputation: the Egyptians will hear. His concern is for God’s name among the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree that Moses argues from God’s glory. This is a model of prayer that appeals to God’s own purposes. This is shared ground.

verses.text: They will tell it to the inhabitants of this land. They have heard that you LORD are among this people; for you LORD are seen face to face, and your cloud stands over them, and you go before them, in a pillar of cloud by day, and in a pillar of fire by night.
verses.arminianNotes: Moses notes that the nations know the LORD is among Israel, seen “face to face,” with his cloud and pillar of fire. God’s presence with Israel is public knowledge, so its outcome reflects on him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers read the verse the same way. Moses grounds his plea in God’s visible covenant presence. This is shared ground.

verses.text: Now if you killed this people as one man, then the nations which have heard the fame of you will speak, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: If God kills the people “as one man,” the nations will draw a conclusion. Moses’ argument assumes that God’s actions bear witness to his character.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers agree. The prayer appeals to God’s concern for his glory among the nations. If Israel were killed “as one man,” Moses argues, the peoples who have already heard the LORD’s fame would misread the act.

This is shared ground.

verses.text: ‘Because the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land which he swore to them, therefore he has slain them in the wilderness.’
verses.arminianNotes: The nations would say the LORD was not able to bring Israel into the land. Moses argues that God’s power, not only his patience, is at stake.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note the same reasoning. Moses’ intercession rests on God’s own honor. The imagined taunt—“the LORD was not able to bring this people into the land which he swore to them”—is what Moses will not have the nations say.

This is shared ground.

verses.text: Now please let the power of the Lord be great, according as you have spoken, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Moses asks that the Lord’s power be great “according as you have spoken.” He appeals to God’s own word. Arminian readers see prayer that takes God at his revealed character.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see prayer that pleads God’s promises back to him. Moses asks that the Lord’s power be great “according as you have spoken,” tying the request to words God has already given, not to a new standard of Moses’ own.

This is shared ground.

verses.text: ‘The LORD is slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness, forgiving iniquity and disobedience; and he will by no means clear the guilty, visiting the iniquity of the fathers on the children, on the third and on the fourth generation.’
verses.arminianNotes: Moses quotes God’s self-revelation from Exodus 34:6–7: slow to anger, abundant in loving kindness, forgiving, yet not clearing the guilty. Mercy and justice stand together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also see the Sinai revelation as the foundation of the plea. Both traditions note that the outcome of this chapter displays both halves of this description: pardon and judgment.

verses.text: Please pardon the iniquity of this people according to the greatness of your loving kindness, and just as you have forgiven this people, from Egypt even until now.”
verses.arminianNotes: Moses asks God to pardon the people according to his loving kindness, as he has from Egypt until now. His appeal is to God’s consistent past mercy.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers read this as a model of intercession grounded in God’s steadfast love. Moses asks for pardon “according to the greatness of your loving kindness,” and he points to the mercy already shown “from Egypt even until now.”

This is shared ground.

verses.text: The LORD said, “I have pardoned according to your word;
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD answers, “I have pardoned according to your word.” Classical Arminian readers hold that God genuinely responds to prayer. Because God foreknows the prayer, he can include it in his plans, so the change is real at the level of God’s dealings without implying he learned something new. They distinguish this from open theism, which denies exhaustive foreknowledge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers hold that God’s purpose does not change, and that he ordains prayer as the means by which he brings his purposes about. The language of relenting describes God’s real response as it appears in history, without implying a change in his eternal decree. They affirm that Moses’ prayer truly mattered.
verses.keyContrast: Both classical traditions affirm that God foreknows all things, that Moses’ prayer was real and effective, and that God does not change in his character. The difference lies in how God’s plan and the prayer relate. Classical Arminians typically say God, foreseeing Moses’ free intercession, planned his response to it. Reformed interpreters typically say God decreed both the intercession and the pardon, ordaining the prayer as the means to his purpose. Neither tradition reads the verse as God learning something new or changing his mind in an open-theist sense.

verses.text: but in very deed—as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with the LORD’s glory—
verses.arminianNotes: Pardon is immediately followed by an oath: “as I live,” all the earth will be filled with the LORD’s glory. God’s mercy does not cancel his purpose to be glorified. The nation is spared, but the rebellion will not go unanswered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s glory as the goal of both pardon and judgment. The oath “as I live, and as all the earth shall be filled with the LORD’s glory” follows the pardon, so mercy does not cancel God’s purpose to be known in all the earth.

This is shared ground.

verses.text: because all those men who have seen my glory and my signs, which I worked in Egypt and in the wilderness, yet have tempted me these ten times, and have not listened to my voice;
verses.arminianNotes: The men who saw God’s glory and signs in Egypt and the wilderness have tested him “these ten times.” Interpreters differ on whether ten is a literal count or a way of saying “many times.” Either way, their sin is against great light.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same uncertainty about the number and the same weight of responsibility. This is shared ground.

verses.text: surely they shall not see the land which I swore to their fathers, neither shall any of those who despised me see it.
verses.arminianNotes: God swears that those who despised him will not see the land promised to their fathers. Hebrews 3–4 applies this to the Christian life as a warning. Arminian readers note that those who fell had genuinely been redeemed from Egypt and had witnessed God’s works, which they see as showing how serious falling away is.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also take the warning in Hebrews seriously. They note that the generation’s exclusion was from the land, a temporal inheritance; how Hebrews applies this warning is taken up at verse 29. Both traditions agree the warning must be heeded.

verses.text: But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and has followed me fully, him I will bring into the land into which he went. His offspring shall possess it.
verses.arminianNotes: Caleb is set apart because he had “another spirit” and followed the LORD fully. He and his offspring will inherit the land. Arminian readers see wholehearted faith and obedience rewarded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Caleb’s different spirit as the fruit of God’s grace in him. Both traditions honor Caleb’s faithfulness and see God keeping his word to the faithful.

verses.text: Since the Amalekite and the Canaanite dwell in the valley, tomorrow turn and go into the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea.”
verses.arminianNotes: With the Amalekites and Canaanites in the valley, Israel must turn back toward the wilderness by the way to the Red Sea. The journey reverses: they head away from the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the same reversal. Unbelief turns the people back from the very edge of the promise. This is shared ground.
